And how does it work? Or is it a complete mystery?

Gravity is best explained historically...let's see how much I can remember.

Newton's concept of gravity was that of an instantaneous force acting between two objects. In this model, it is best to think of gravity as a rope connecting two objects: (in this model) if the Sun were to disappear, the Earth would fly off in a straight line instantly. Newton's Theory of Gravity was enough to land astronauts/rovers on the moon back in the day. But it is an incomplete theory. And it doesn't say anything about what gravity is.

One thing that spelled failure for Newton's laws was the precession of the perihelion of Mercury (henceforth PPM). I'll edit this post with links a little later. The PPM is the actual shift in orientation of Mercuries orbit around the Sun, which is not fully accounted for in Newtonian gravity. It is however explained by General Relativity (GR). But before I move on to GR I want to bring something else up. If the Sun disappears in Newtonian gravity, we fly off instantly; however, as edumucated 21st centuryites, we know that it takes the light 8 minutes to travel from the Sun to Earth. Well it bothered Einstein that we'd be able to tell that the Sun had disappeared, before we could see it disappear. Especially since he had shown in the early 1900s that the speed of light was a cosmic speed limit. If that is the case how could the Suns gravity be 'communicating' faster than its light?

GR was proposed by Einstein in the 1910s. It puts forth that Gravity is just the warping of "spacetime" and the curved paths we move in space are geodesics (straight lines) on the complex geometry of spacetime. When the Sun is removed from spacetime, the spacetime ripples as it goes to equilibrium, and these ripples or waves travel at the speed of light. So that solves the conceptual problem above. Now when the Sun disappears we'd fly off exactly eight minutes later, right as the lights went out for good. And GR solves the PPM to astounding accuracy.

But it is still not a complete theory. Anything past this point is pure theory.

Particle Physics has been searching for a force carrier for Gravity, called the graviton. If this is discovered it would show that gravity behaves like every other force, through the exchange of force carrying particles at varying strengths.

String Theory proposes that all the fundamental particles of the universe are vibrating strands of energy. All of them closed loops, except for the Strings for gravity which are theorized to be open ended. If String Theory is true...well it just probably isn't...but if it were...well let's just hope it's not.

My favorite is Loop Quantum Gravity. It is IMO the most promising explanation of gravity.

Imagine a bowling ball (mass) placed on a trampoline (an analogy for spacetime). The bowling ball bends the trampoline (spacetime), curving it down, so if you placed another mass on the trampoline, the curved surface then makes the mass "fall" towards each other.

I recently moved and had to tear down my 70 gallon tank since we were going to be living with friends for a couple months waiting to close on the new house.

Before setting the tank back up I was thinking of changing out some components and was wondering what inexpensive canister filters some of you might have some experience with that you could suggest.

I'm thinking about adding a second filter to my 55 gallon, and canisters look like a good option. I like the ability to load them with almost any sort of filter media. I'm in the same boat as you though, there's tons of options and not a lot of info on how they compare. They seem easy enough to build too, and I wonder if anyone here has experience building their own and would like to share how that went.

I paid about $80 for my Eheim 250 and have loved it. I really have no basis for comparison as it's the only canister filter I've ever had. When I was researching, the Eheim and Fluval seemed to be the most highly regarded, and Eheim cost less.
My experience with an Eheim is also pretty solid. Unfortunately, the newer models are made in China which is not nearly as good as the old ones made in Germany
So far so good on my Eheim. I do need to find something to clean the gunk out of the tubes beyond just blowing out what I can...

Sunsun is a solid filter. It's an off-brand (hehe), but we switched from a Rena/API brand filter that had been on my 60gal due to some circumstances. Our Rena filter still works perfectly but it's in another state right now, haha.

We paid 80~ for the Sunsun on Amazon (it just went on sale), here is the specific one if you want to check it out. It comes with a built-in UV light and a surface skimmer (which is kinda weird getting used to, if you mess around in your tank a lot and move the water it tends to get wonky but it fixes itself after a few minutes!) The instructions were very vague but it didn't take me more than like 15 minutes to put it all together and get it set up.
I purchased a sunsun uv sterilizer and it never worked so my experience with them is poor.

Ahh, maybe they're hit and miss then! Mine is working so far so good!

I'd probably recommend API then, since that's the only other brand of filters I've had experience with! Best of luck!
also, has anyone ever used an inline heater as opposed to a hanging heater. I would like to clean up the back wall of the aquarium as much as possible.
I never used an inline heater, but my experience with a hanging heater is that if you hang it vertically at one of the back corners, its barely noticeable.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OxFb3EeZ7l8

Or like this one do it yourself, can make a filter as big as you want. I honestly have been thinking about trying something like this out in the new 220gal I bought, just to see how well it would cycle the water (no fish just cycling and would probably use a 5 gallon gatorade as a canister, if it works will update) just a thought though and it's kinda unique.

I've been using the Cascade 1000 for over a year now. For the price I was very surprised with the quality. The filter runs silent and maintenance is simple. If you want to replace the filter media you can close the input and output streams and disconnect the entire filter from your system. It works surprisingly well and I have yet to spill water while doing this.
No problems with leaks. I have heard mix reviews about the cascade, though it is the one I was leaning toward, mainly because of price.

The manual states a specific procedure when trying to turn off the filter to clean. First you close the valve on the input stream just before the filter. Once you do that then you close the exit stream valve and then turn off the filter. After you do this you can unscrew each of the streams and remove the entire filter. There will be some water inside the canister itself, but it has never been a problem. This is the only canister filter I've ever owned, but I was impressed by how easily you can detach the filter without spilling any water.
do you have an inline uv sterilizer? The Cascade 1000 pumps 265 gph and I haven't found any inline sterilizers that can handle that.
